segments.text: - Hello, everyone.
Welcome back to Altium Academy.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson,

and today, we're gonna be
talking about the thought process

behind picking a stackup,
planning out your routes,
designing your transmission lines,
and getting started with a new design.

Now recently I got a really
great question on my LinkedIn,

and this is really four
different questions,

but when you take these
four questions together,
they really illustrate the thought process
behind picking a stackup for a new design.

We're gonna show some
examples in Altium Designer
that show you how to do this

and what is possible when you
consider the stackup first.
Let's go ahead and get started.
(upbeat music)
So I get tons of great questions
from all of you folks on LinkedIn
and first things first, I wanna say thanks
for sending me those questions.
I know I don't reply to all of 'em,

but sometimes we get a
really great question,
and, of course, it makes it into a video.
This question we're gonna look at
in just a moment relates to stackup design
and the thought process behind it,
especially as it relates to a new design.
Let's take a look at this question.
"Hi, Zach, I hope you were doing well.
"I have a question.

"Maybe you already addressed
this in your videos,

"but it would be great if
you can give me some insight.

"I have to design a board
based on an LTE module

"and a lower module along
with some power circuitry."

Ali then goes into four
different questions here
that relate to stackup design,
as well as a routing question
about RF routing for an antenna.
Now in looking at those four questions,

I see that Ali is trying to
figure out the overall process
for designing a stackup
and planning out routing for a new design,

in particular, one that
uses both power circuitry,

which is pretty typical,
as well as some RF.

Now because he's using a lower
module and an LTE module,

there are also gonna be some
digital signals on this board.

What I wanna do is
address these one by one,

and we'll look at some
examples in Altium Designer
as we go through this.
Let's take a look at question one.

"What is the best stackup
for such a design?"

Well, there are many different
stackups that you could use.

For example, you could
use a standard stackup
from a manufacturer.

You could, of course,
design your own stackup
from commercially available materials.

What I'm gonna do is show
you an example design

and talk through the thought
process behind the stackup,
and then hopefully that will illustrate
what you should do in your design.

Now here I have on screen a
design that uses an LTE module,
and it includes an antenna on the board
and it has some RF routing.

So it also has some power
circuitry making it pretty similar
to what you need to do in your design.

Now folks who have been
reading the Altium blog
for a while probably recognize this board.

This is a variant of the
LTE GNSS tracker project
from Mark Harris.
This was adapted by a client of mine,

and we helped them make
it into a custom design.

So if you wanna learn more
about the original project,
head over to the link in the description.
You'll see a blog link there,
and go ahead and read about this project.
Now I have the stackup pulled up here,
and you can see the type of stackup

that you should use for
this type of project.

Here, what I've shown
is a 4-layer stackup,

and I think that's gonna
be the entry level stackup
that you should use in your design,

which, again, is also
based on an LTE module

and has some digital
stuff and power circuitry.

So it's very similar to
what we're looking at now.
Here what I've pulled up on the stackup
is you can see the layer thicknesses
that are being used here.
Now these layer thicknesses correspond
to thin outer layers of prepreg,
and then you have a thick core layer
that separates our two planes.
Now why use a 4-layer board?
Well, here on this 4-layer board,

you can see that we have
thin outer layers of prepreg

on the top and bottom, and then
we have a thick core layer.

Now there are a couple of
reasons that we want to do this.
One of the reasons is that

we can apply impedance
control, and you can see here

that I have the impedance
calculator pulled up,
and I'll explain the settings

for the impedance
calculator in just a moment.
The other reason that we do that
is because, of course, there's going
to be some digital stuff on this board.

This is going to ensure that
we have tight return paths

in the planes on layer
two and layer three,

and that's going to help
reduce radiated emissions,
as well as EMI susceptibility.
This is also beneficial for power.
It's going to help ensure that any noise

from switching circuits
is going to be contained

in the PCB, and it will
reduce radiated emissions
from those noisy switching circuits.

Now let's look at the
impedance for just a moment.

On layer one, we've
applied impedance control

as a co-planner configuration
with 50 Ohm target impedance,

and that is going to be for
these antenna feed lines.

You can see we have
one antenna right here,

and then we have another
antenna right here,
and we wanna make sure that we have both

of those antenna feed
lines set to 50 Ohms.
Now if you look here, you can see
that we have some pretty tight spacing

between the ground on the
top layer and the trace,

and if we put this in 3D, we
can see how this is routed.
You can see here on layer two
that we have a cutout below that trace,

and then the ground reference
is set here on layer three.
So that's what we've set up here
inside the impedance calculator.

You can see here that
we've set the reference
here for layer three,

and you see here the
name it says layer two,

but the layer number is
actually layer three.
Pay attention to that.
And then we can see here
what the width is calculated to be.
And then we have a clearance value

that we've set here in
the impedance calculator.
Now, the reason we do this
is because even on a 4-layer board
targeting 50 Ohms impedance,

we're still able to use a
wide trace if we need it.

And because this is a design
that's using LTE and GNSS,
we wanna make sure we have a wider trace
that's going to reduce the losses

for that RF signal that's
coming into the board
and is received by those antennas.

Hopefully this covers
everything you need to know
from the electrical functionality side
and, of course, the EMI EMC side
and some aspects of signal integrity.
Now let's look at question two.

"What factors define
selection of the stackup
"other than and form factors?"
This is another great question.

How do we select anything
that goes into the stackup?

Well, I think there are a
couple of ways to do this.

Of course, you could start
with a standard stackup
from your fabrication house,

and this is exactly what
we did in this design.

So what I'm gonna do is
head over to a webpage here,
which shows the standard stackup

from Circuit Hub that
we used in this design.

If I just scroll down
to their 4-layer area,

you can see that we have
the stackup that was used

and defined in Altium
Designer for this design.
And if we just scroll up a little bit,

you see here the materials
that they have available
for use in these designs.

Now we already see one
important material parameter
in these material entries,

and that is the glass
transition temperature.

You can see here for
their normal TG materials,

they are targeting glass
transition temperature
of 130 to 135 degrees Celsius,

and then here we have
the high TG materials
with 170 degrees Celsius.

Now that glass transition
temperature is important

because if the board is
gonna be thermally cycled,

this is going to determine
the level of stress
you can expect when the board temperature
is cycled up to very high values.

And if you need to have a
very high reliability board,
you would want to then select
a high glass transition temperature.
Now, sometimes, of course,
the standard stackup won't work for you,

and you might need to
select your own materials

and layer thicknesses in
order to complete the design.

That usually relates to
components and especially BGAs.

Sometimes with BGAs, you may
have a very fine pitch BGA,
and we're gonna see an example of that
here shortly in this video,
but that fine pitch BGA could dictate

that you use blind and
buried vias for routing.

That, of course, is going to
limit the material thicknesses
that you can use in the stackup
because you have aspect ratio limits
that you have to obey when working
with those types of components
and that type of routing.

What are some other
parameters we might need

to consider when selecting
materials for a stackup?
Well, one of these could be,
for example, reliability at high voltages.
Not all PCBs are used at low voltage DC.
Sometimes they're used at high voltage DC
or high voltage AC.
And of course, there are some different

performance level
classifications that are used
to quantify acceptable performance
at various voltage ranges.

I have included the
performance level categories

for high voltage PCB
materials in this blog.
Go ahead and check out the link
in the description to read this blog

and learn more about
high voltage materials.
In high reliability boards,

the curing agent that
is used in the material
also influences reliability
because it influences the growth
of conductive and nautic filamentation.
If we scroll down here,
we can see some data compiled from Isola.

This data shows the failure
rate for different materials
that use different types of curing agents.
Here we have a phenolic cured material,
and then here we have a DC cured material,

and you can see here that
the phenolic cured material
has a much lower failure rate
for different wall-to-wall separations
for structures in the PCB.
Now, I could keep going with this,
but, of course, we've already addressed
some of these aspects in another video
on PCB material constructions.
So make sure to check out the link
in the video description and learn more.

Now, let's take a look
at Ali's third question.

"What books or material can
help me get a stronghold
"on these concepts?"
Well, I would recommend you head over
to education.altium.com.

You can sign up for
Altium Education for free,
and if you are an active student

with a valid educational
institution email address,

you can get a student
license of Altium Designer.

You don't have to be a student
to use Altium Education.
Anybody can sign up with an email address
and start learning for free.

Now, let's take a look
at Ali's fourth question.
"I have to route the trace for an antenna.
"I know it should have 50 Ohm impedance
"and be a microstrip.
"What important factors should I consider
"while creating it?"
Well, to answer that question,

let's jump back into
the Mark Harris design,

and we'll briefly look
at one of my designs
that we've shown in an earlier video.

First in the Mark Harris
design, you can see here
that if we just put this into 2D, again,
we have an important consideration,
which is the routing style.
It's not just done as microstrip,

but it's actually done as a
grounded coplanar waveguide.
The reason that's done
is because applying this via fencing
along this coplanar waveguide
provides some shielding effectiveness,
and it helps confine the RF signal
into the region around this trace.
The next thing you should consider

is whether or not you have
any cutout below this trace.
Now, you can see here in single layer mode
that we do have a cutout on layer two,

and then we have the
ground here on layer three.

Now, the reason that we've
done that in this design

is, of course, it allows
that trace to be wider,
which reduces the losses

while the signal propagates
along that trace.
Now, there's another reason we may want

to have this cutout in
these internal layers,
and it relates to parasitics
in the impedance matching network.

So let's take a look at
the NRF52 module project,

which I showed in an earlier
video on the channel.
Here, if we put this into 3D
and we turn on single layer mode,
you can see as I scroll through the layers

that we have a cutout passing
through the internal layers,
and eventually we have our completion
of ground on layer six.
This is also done as a coplanar waveguide,
and it's for the same reasons

that I talked about in
the Mark Harris project.
Now, one of the reasons this was done

in this design was,
first, it does allow us
to use a wider trace if needed,
and, of course, that is beneficial

because we are routing
into a wider trace antenna,

and it allows us to reduce some
of the loss along this line.
However, this is not a very long line,
and you can see here that we're routing
directly into some components
for an impedance matching network,
specifically a CLC filter.

Now, you can see here in these
capacitors, in this inductor
that the pads are quite large,

and so it makes sense to
size the trace to correspond
to the width of those pads.

However, you can see that
when we have these large pads,
it creates some additional parasitics
due to the presence of ground nearby,
and that slightly modifies the performance
of this impedance matching network
once you put it into the PCB layout.

So what that means is
that the cutoff frequency

that you calculate from
the circuit is not going
to be the same cutout frequency
that you actually observe in the PCB.
In order to reduce these parasitics,
we can use that ground cutout
as I've shown here in this design.

If you wanna learn more about
the process for this design,

take a look at the video
link in the description.

I described this design in
much more detail in that video.

Now, the last important
factor is whether or not

you actually need an
impedance matching network.
Now, for your particular project
where you have an LTE module,

you may not need an
impedance matching network
because the output impedance

of your module could already
be matched to your antenna,
which is most likely 50 Ohms.

However, in this case where
we're using an NRF52 module,

the output impedance from
this NRF52 is not 50 Ohms.

I think it's more like 30
plus 35 Ohms of reactants.
I'd have to look in the data sheet,

but you actually see
something similar with ESP32.
So it's actually quite common

that the output impedance
at these frequencies

where you're dealing
with, for example, LTE
or Bluetooth, is not exactly 50 Ohms.
So make sure to check the data sheet
and make sure you actually need
to apply an impedance matching network
before just sticking one in the design.
Thanks, everyone, for watching this video,
and thank you, Ali Khan,

for sending me those great
questions on LinkedIn.
If you guys have questions or comments,

make sure to leave them
in the comments section,

and they might just appear
in one of these videos.
Make sure to hit that Like button,
hit that Subscribe button,

and don't forget to call
your fabricator, folks.
We'll see you next time.
